TrusTrace released a new report finding that 21% of surveyed fashion brands selling into the United States have had a shipment detained by U.S. Customs and Border Protection . The report also found that 75% are not fully prepared to prove where their materials came from when asked.
What’s Related
The report, The Enforcement Era: Fashion’s Compliance Readiness in Numbers , examines how brands collect supplier information, monitor compliance , and prepare documentation. TrusTrace launched it at the Textile Exchange Conference in Vancouver.
The report found a sharp drop in trusted supplier information beyond the factories making finished products. While 75% of surveyed brands reported trusted data at that first supplier level, only 20% had it at the raw material and farm level.
Where brands are missing supplier information
Other findings show where respondents face gaps:
Shipment detention risk : Among U.S.-selling brands that had not experienced a detention, 58% considered it a realistic near-term risk.
Upstream supplier information: Trusted data fell to 33% at Tier 3, which covers yarn and fiber, before dropping further at the raw material level.
Supplier screening : Nearly half (48%) of U.S.-selling respondents had not screened suppliers against U.S. government forced labor entity lists.
Compliance monitoring: Only 21% reported continuous, automated compliance checks across suppliers, while 17% still relied on spreadsheets and email.
Digital product passports: Although 69% were actively preparing for digital product passports, that group rated its supply chain data accuracy at a median of three out of five.
“Enforcement is no longer on the horizon. It is here. Border officials look at evidence to decide which goods move and which goods they hold,” said Shameek Ghosh, CEO and Co-Founder of TrusTrace.
Suppliers need clearer documentation guidance
Supplier resistance or limited capability was the most frequently cited barrier, named by 60% of respondents. Meanwhile, 63% identified industry-wide supplier data standards as a way to speed progress, making it the most selected option.
The report includes interviews with Brooks Running, a TrusTrace customer, and U.S. apparel group Komar. It also included Christian Hudson of the UN Center for Trade Facilitation and Julie Robertson of PIP Global Safety.
“The hardest part is that there is no single right answer for what a complete document set looks like at each level of the supply chain, which makes it genuinely difficult for suppliers to know how much is enough,” said Tahagod Mohamed, Senior Traceability Analyst at Brooks Running.
“Our guidance to them is simple: provide as much as you can to show how the raw material was produced, processed, transported , and paid for to make the final product,” Mohamed said.
The survey received 57 responses across 24 countries during the first half of 2026, including 40 fully completed surveys. Participants included sustainability directors, compliance leads, supply chain heads, and C-suite executives, along with a small number of manufacturers , mills and industry organizations. Percentages were calculated using only those who answered each question, with sample sizes ranging from 24 to 55.
Ways to improve readiness
The report outlines five stages for improving readiness: identify suppliers, trace materials back to their origin, connect information across company functions, automate compliance monitoring, and prepare documentation for review. The framework draws on practices from brands the report identifies as furthest ahead.
Its proposed 90-day agenda includes assessing how much reliable information a company holds at each supplier level, screening against entity lists, and testing whether it can assemble the documentation needed to respond to a CBP inquiry.
